name: command-message
intent: Use a message whose payload names the operation to perform and its arguments to reliably ask exactly one receiver to do something, so a caller can invoke behavior across a process, language or ownership boundary without binding to the receiver's interface, address or lifecycle.
problem: A caller needs an operation that only another component can perform - because that component owns the data, the device or the capability - but a direct call would bind the caller to the receiver's location, technology and availability, and a lost call cannot be retried. How can the work be requested as data, so that routing, timing and failure handling become the channel's business while the receiver stays the single owner of the operation?
context: Distributed integration or in-process command buses where work must be requested across a trust or process boundary, the caller does not need the result immediately, and the channel can provide store-and-forward, retry or at-least-once delivery. Applies when the set of operations can be named as versioned data and the receiver - not the sender - owns the state the command changes; synchronous user-facing calls and broadcast notifications belong to other patterns.
benefits: Decouples caller and receiver in time, location and technology: the receiver may be offline, replaced or relocated while the command waits in the channel.
Distributes work naturally: a point-to-point channel with competing consumers load-balances commands across a receiver pool, and each command is delivered to one of them.
Keeps the business rules in one place - the component that owns the data executes the command, so invariants are enforced where the state lives and the sender cannot corrupt it.
Commands are data: they can be persisted, audited, replayed, delayed, scheduled, routed by content and inspected without exercising the receiver.
Adds operational resilience through channel features: redelivery, dead-letter channels and retry policies apply to a failed command without the sender resending it.
Makes intent explicit on the wire: the operation is named in the message, unlike in a document or event whose meaning the receiver must infer.
tradeoffs: At-least-once delivery executes the same command more than once unless the receiver is idempotent or deduplicates; the pattern itself provides no exactly-once semantics.

Without an explicit reply the sender cannot distinguish 'failed' from 'not processed yet'; adding Request-Reply restores correlation, timeouts and reply-channel bookkeeping - and the coupling that comes with them.
A command message is a remote call in disguise: fine-grained, setter-style commands produce chatty traffic, added latency and a distributed monolith.
The payload is a versioned wire contract: renaming a command, changing its parameters or removing a type breaks messages already in the channel, so commands must evolve compatibly.

Authority travels as data: whoever can publish to the command channel can ask the receiver to act, so authentication, authorization and schema validation at the receiver are mandatory rather than optional.
End-to-end visibility drops: the caller gets no stack trace, and diagnosing a command means correlating broker, consumer and handler logs by an identifier the sender had to add itself.

participants.responsibility: The data that names the operation and carries its parameters; with the message headers it is the whole request, and its type tag (discriminator) is what the receiver dispatches on.
Creates the command payload, wraps it in a message with the needed headers, and sends it to the command channel; it usually does not know which receiver instance will execute it.
Envelope of headers plus body: headers carry routing, correlation, expiry and reply metadata while the body carries the command.
Point-to-point transport between sender and receiver; together with the broker it provides persistence, single-consumer semantics and redelivery.
Consumer plumbing that listens on the channel, deserializes the message, validates the discriminator and schema, and hands the command to the handler.
Executes the operation against the state it owns, and decides the idempotency, retry and error policy; the only place that mutates that state.
Carries a result or domain error back when the caller needs the outcome; used with Return Address and Correlation Identifier.

use_cases: Requesting work from the service that owns the data (reserve stock, charge a card, ship an order), so only that service mutates its state.
Handing long-running or non-interactive work to a worker pool: report generation, media transcoding, batch imports, e-mail dispatch.
Controlling devices and field equipment - open a valve, reboot a node, set a setpoint - where the target answers slowly or not at all.
Wrapping procedures of a legacy system (a mainframe transaction, an ERP function module) behind a message channel so callers do not speak its protocol.
In-process command buses and worker threads, where command objects are queued for another thread to execute.
Saga and process-manager steps that must invoke a participant - compensations included - as discrete, retryable units of work.
Administrative and operational control: purge a queue, reset a counter, toggle a feature via a control channel.
Cross-aggregate commands in DDD: when one business transaction spans multiple aggregates, issue separate commands to each aggregate's owner rather than reaching across boundaries directly.
CQRS write-side operations: commands arriving from API handlers or event-triggered workflows that represent intent to change domain state.
Wrapping third-party or SaaS API calls behind a command channel so the sender is decoupled from the vendor's availability and can benefit from retry and circuit-breaker policies.

RabbitMQ work queues (task queues): the sender encapsulates a task as a message on one queue and competing consumers pull it round-robin; manual acknowledgment plus basic.qos(prefetch=1) give fair dispatch and redeliver the command when a worker dies.

Celery distributed task queue: invoking a task publishes a message carrying only the task name and arguments to a broker, and a worker looks the callable up in its registry and executes it - a command message dispatched by name tag, made retry-safe with acks_late and idempotent tasks.

Amazon SQS work queues: producers send command messages to a managed queue, the visibility timeout hides in-flight commands from competing consumers, and a dead-letter queue gives poison commands an explicit fate.
avoid_when: The receiver is in the same process and the operation returns quickly: a method call, a Method Object or a local dispatcher is simpler and gives real error semantics.
The caller needs the result inside a user-facing request/response cycle: a synchronous call (HTTP, gRPC) has fewer moving parts than messaging plus Request-Reply.
You are announcing a fact to whoever cares: use Event Message on a publish-subscribe channel - a command sent to many receivers executes the same work many times.
You only need to move data: a Document Message (or a Data Transfer Object across a Remote Facade) says that honestly.

The operation must not be retried or duplicated and the channel offers only at-least-once delivery with no deduplication store: make the receiver idempotent first, or use a single-attempt request/reply channel.
anti_patterns: Command as remote procedure call: hundreds of fine-grained setter-style commands mirroring the receiver's private methods, coupling the sender to internal structure and turning the integration into a distributed monolith.
Publishing a command on a publish-subscribe channel, so that every subscriber executes it while each one believes it is the only receiver.
A command on an at-least-once channel with a non-idempotent handler and no deduplication, presented as reliable delivery.
Naming the command in the past tense (OrderPlaced) so receivers treat it as a notification; the sender's intent disappears and duplicates or unmet preconditions go unchecked.
Shipping a host-language object (Java ObjectMessage, .NET BinaryFormatter) whose deserialization exists only on the sender's runtime, binding both sides to one version of one platform.
Using a command for what is actually a query: a command that returns domain data on the success path couples the write model to the read model and erodes the CQRS boundary.
design_principles: Tell, don't ask: a command states the intent to change something, and the receiver decides how - the sender does not read state across the boundary and write it back.
Single writer / information ownership: only the component that owns the state executes the command that changes it.
Separation of interface from implementation: the message contract (operation plus parameters) is independent of the receiver's classes, language and deployment.
Explicit boundaries: the operation is named data on the wire, so the contract is documented and versioned instead of being implied by a call stack.
Least authority at the boundary: the receiver authorizes each command as a request from an untrusted peer, never as an internal call.
Imperative naming: command names are active verbs in the present tense (ReserveStock, not StockReserved or StockReservation), making intent unmistakable on the wire.
best_practices: Name commands as imperative domain operations (ReserveStock, not UpdateStockReservationRow) and give each command exactly one receiver so the point-to-point channel stays honest.
Make command handling idempotent or deduplicate on a stable key (command id, business id, message id) - real brokers deliver at least once.
Validate and authorize at the receiver: check the discriminator, the schema version and the sender's rights before executing anything.
Version the payload: additive fields, tolerant deserialization and a compatibility rule for removed command types; keep old names working until in-flight messages have drained.
Keep commands small and self-contained (identifiers plus the data needed, or a Claim Check reference) and never ship live objects, connections or file handles.
Give a command an explicit fate: dead-letter channel plus alerting for commands no handler accepts, and a correlated reply with a timeout when the caller needs confirmation.
Keep the discriminator canonical across the system: one tag field name and one naming convention for its values.
When a command handler also publishes events, use the transactional outbox so the state change and the outgoing message commit atomically.
Supply an idempotency key on every command from the caller: store it alongside the business effect in the same transaction so redelivery is detected before the handler runs again.
Use a composite deduplication key (both broker message-id and a business-level idempotency key) to catch both broker-level redelivery and producer-level replays.

Enforce that commands have a single logical owner: if multiple handler instances can process the same command type on the same channel, deduplication records must be keyed to the consumer identity as well as the message identity.

Distinguish command validation (request-level: is the payload well-formed, are required fields present?) from domain validation (can this operation succeed given current state?) - do not conflate the two.
In saga orchestration, model each step as a discrete command with a corresponding compensating command; ensure every step is idempotent since sagas are inherently retry-driven.
When wrapping a legacy system, model the command after the business operation, not after the legacy API surface - the command is the contract, the wrapper translates.
